The upcoming MacBook Ultra will definitely not come cheap, with an all-new slim design, OLED display, and touch functionality — and that’s before factoring in price hikes driven by rising memory costs. The latest reports suggest manufacturing costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple has always preferred to source components from multiple suppliers to ensure a stable display supply and secure the best pricing, and had originally hoped to continue this strategy with the MacBook Ultra. However, supply chain sources have revealed that Apple has ultimately decided to use only a single display supplier…

The screens for Apple’s products are handled by three partners: Samsung, LG, and BOE. Among them, BOE has so far only supplied displays for the company’s lower-end products, while high-end display orders are shared between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature the most sophisticated display Apple has ever produced. Combining tandem OLED with touch functionality and scaling it up to the larger sizes required for laptops is no easy feat. The latest supply chain report indicates that Apple has decided to exclusively source these displays from Samsung.

According to The Elec, LG failed to meet the production volumes required by Apple.

Apple required large-area substrates for mass production. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6th-generation OLED production line, while LG Display reportedly explored using its existing 6th-generation line. Even though producing laptop OLED displays on a 6th-generation line is technically feasible, substrate efficiency and productivity are lower than on the 8.6th-generation line. Because initial production volumes were low, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as its sole supplier.

It seems LG can only offer limited production capacity, and the logistical complexity of dealing with two suppliers isn’t worth it. LG is not expected to potentially supply displays for this flagship MacBook until as late as 2029.

This arrangement clearly gives Samsung stronger bargaining leverage on panel pricing. This situation is expected to drive up Apple’s manufacturing costs and, just like the rising memory costs, will ultimately be passed on to consumers.

Given that the MacBook Ultra’s price could be staggeringly high, how interested are you in considering an upgrade? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
